section.title: Let All Creation Praise the Lord
section.sectionRationale: The third Hallelujah psalm summons all creation, heavens and earth alike, angels, sun, moon, stars, sea creatures, weather, mountains, trees, animals, and every class of human being, to praise the LORD who created and sustains them all, and who has raised up a horn, a rescuer king, for His people, foreshadowing Revelation 5:13's vision of every creature praising the Lamb.
section.thesis: All creation, from the highest heavens to the depths of the sea, exists to praise its Maker, and its worship is fulfilled when creation's Redeemer, who raised up a horn of salvation for His people, receives, with all creation, unending praise.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the heavens summoned to praise, verses 1-6; the earth summoned to praise, verses 7-10; and every class of humanity summoned to praise, culminating in the horn raised up for Israel, verses 11-14.

units.label: Praise Him, all His angels
units.note: the heavens summoned to praise their Creator

verses.text: {{haleluyah|Hallelujah}}! Praise the LORD from the heavens; praise Him in the highest places.
Praise Him, all His angels; praise Him, all His heavenly {{tsava|hosts}}.
Praise Him, O sun and moon; praise Him, all you shining stars.
Praise Him, O highest heavens, and you waters above the skies.
Let them praise the name of the LORD, for He gave the command and they were created.
He established them forever and ever; He issued a decree that will never pass away.

units.label: Praise the Lord from the earth
units.note: sea creatures, weather, mountains, trees, and animals summoned to praise

verses.text: Praise the LORD from the earth, all great sea creatures and ocean depths,
lightning and hail, snow and clouds, powerful wind fulfilling His word,
mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars,
wild animals and all cattle, crawling creatures and flying birds,

units.label: Let them praise the name of the Lord
units.note: every human summoned, and Israel's horn of salvation

verses.text: kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all rulers of the earth,
young men and maidens, old and young together.
Let them praise the name of the LORD, for His name alone is exalted; His splendor is above the earth and the heavens.
He has raised up a {{qeren|horn}} for His people, the praise of all His saints, of Israel, a people near to Him. {{haleluyah|Hallelujah}}!

haleluyah.gloss: An imperative call, praise the LORD. It opens and closes each of the last five psalms of the Psalter, framing the whole collection's final movement as one continuous shout of praise.

tsava.gloss: Host or army; the ranks of heavenly beings who serve and worship God, summoned here alongside sun, moon, and stars to praise their Maker.

qeren.gloss: Horn, a symbol of strength and victory drawn from an animal's horn. The LORD raises up a horn, a rescuer king, for His people; Zechariah's song applies the same image directly to Jesus, a horn of salvation, Luke 1:69.

basic.context: This psalm summons the entire created order, from angels and stars to sea creatures, weather, mountains, animals, and every class of human being, to praise the LORD. Its reason is twofold, He created and established them by His command, and His name alone is exalted above earth and heaven.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a hymn of universal praise. The command for non-speaking creation to praise God is not literal speech but a poetic summons, calling humanity, the one part of creation with a voice, to give words to what the rest of creation silently displays.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm opens and closes with haleluyah. Verse 2 summons the tsava, the heavenly hosts, alongside the angels. Verse 14 declares that God has raised up a qeren, a horn, strength and a rescuer, for His people, an image the New Testament applies directly to Jesus.
basic.typology: The horn raised up for God's people, verse 14, anticipates Zechariah's prophecy over his son John the Baptist, that God has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David, Luke 1:69, a horn fulfilled in Jesus the Messiah.
basic.christ: Colossians 1:16-17 identifies Christ as the one by whom and for whom all things were created and in whom all things hold together, the very truth this psalm celebrates in verses 5-6. He is also the horn of salvation raised up for God's people, Luke 1:69, and the one before whom, with the Lamb, all creation will finally sing, Revelation 5:13.
basic.god: God is Creator and Sustainer of everything that exists, in the heavens and on the earth, established by His command and decree. His name alone is exalted above earth and heaven, and He has drawn Israel near to Himself, raising up strength and salvation for His people.
basic.crossReferences: Colossians 1:16-17 identifies Christ as Creator and Sustainer of all things, matching verses 5-6. Luke 1:69 applies this psalm's image of a raised-up horn directly to Jesus. Revelation 5:13 pictures the psalm's summons fulfilled, every creature in heaven and on earth praising God and the Lamb.
basic.oneStory: All creation exists to display God's glory and, through human voices, to praise its Maker. That praise finds its Redeemer and its center in Christ, through whom all things were made, and who is Himself the horn of salvation raised up for God's people, until the day every creature joins the unending song.

context.literary:
Psalm 148 is built like a pair of facing staircases. Verses 1 to 6 call on the heavens and verses 7 to 14 call on the earth, and each half begins with the same command, 'Praise the LORD from' the heavens, then 'from the earth.' Within each half the summons moves through a roll call of beings, and each roll call is rounded off with a reason introduced by 'for' in verses 5 and 13. The psalm teaches by listing, and the lists are arranged with care.

The heavenly list moves from persons to lights to places. Angels and hosts come first, then sun, moon, and stars, then the highest heavens and the waters above the skies, which belong to the three-layered picture of the sky in Genesis 1:6-8. The earthly list moves from the deep to the height and then back to people. It starts with the sea creatures and ocean depths, climbs through lightning, hail, snow, cloud, and wind to mountains and hills, comes down to fruit trees and cedars, and then to wild animals, cattle, crawling things, and birds, which are the living creatures of Genesis 1:20-25. The last and longest list is of people, from kings to children, in verses 11 and 12. People are named last because they are the ones who can speak the praise that the others display. The lists borrow the vocabulary of Genesis 1, which is no accident: the psalm is a roll call of the days of creation turned into worship.

The many pairs and merisms give the sense of totality. 'Kings and all peoples,' 'princes and all rulers,' 'young men and maidens,' and 'old and young' are pairs that cover the whole of humanity from top to bottom and from youngest to oldest. The psalm's reach is the claim that nothing is left outside the praise. The ending is a surprise. After ordering the cosmos to sing, the psalm closes in verse 14 with a small particular: a horn raised up for a people near to Him. The grandest chorus ends with the care of the Creator for one nation, and this is where the psalm's weight finally lands.
context.historical:
To a first hearer in the ancient Near East, the first half of the psalm would have been startling. Sun, moon, and stars were gods or divine beings in the religions of Israel's neighbours, and the sea monsters and deep were forces that the gods had to subdue. Psalm 148 gathers them all into the same list as cattle and fruit trees, and addresses them as creatures that are told to praise. The sun and moon, which Egypt and Mesopotamia worshipped, are put in the pew. Genesis 1:14-16 had already said that the sun and moon are lamps God made and set in the sky, and Deuteronomy 4:19 warned Israel not to be drawn into bowing down to them. Psalm 148 turns the warning into worship by giving the heavenly bodies their proper place as servants who sing.

The 'great sea creatures' of verse 7 use the same word as Genesis 1:21, where God makes them as part of creation. In other cultures the sea monster was an enemy of the gods, and in some Israelite poetry the idea of a monster is borrowed to show God's victory, but here the monsters of the deep are simply asked to join the praise. There is no battle. The text does not say that these beings are hostile powers needing defeat, but that they are creatures.

The mention of kings, princes, and rulers in verse 11 would have had a political edge. Every nation around Israel treated its king as semi-divine or as a representative of the gods. The psalm summons them to stand beside the young men and maidens and to praise the name of the LORD, with the people they rule. Psalm 72:11 pictures kings bowing to Israel's king, Psalm 138:4-5 pictures the kings of the earth giving thanks, and Isaiah 60:3 pictures kings coming to the light.

The psalm gives no title and no date. Its closing words about a horn raised up for a people near to Him suggest a community that has known weakness, and many readers think of the days after the exile, but the psalm is timeless in its wording and works for any age.
context.canonical:
Psalm 148 is the voice of the Psalter's last chapter, and it draws on the whole Bible's account of creation. The commanding word behind verses 5 and 6, 'He gave the command and they were created,' is the voice of Genesis 1, and Psalm 33:6 and 33:9 say that the heavens were made by the word of the LORD and that 'He spoke, and it came to be.' The fixed decree that does not pass away stands beside Psalm 119:89-91 and Jeremiah 31:35-36 and 33:25-26, where the order of sun, moon, and stars is the guarantee that God's covenant with Israel will not be dropped.

The summons to creation to sing has several companions. Psalm 19:1-4 says that the heavens declare the glory of God without speech or language. Psalm 96:11-13 and 98:7-9 call on the sea, the fields, the trees, and the rivers to rejoice before the LORD because He is coming to judge the earth. Isaiah 44:23 and 55:12 summon the heavens, the mountains, and the trees to sing and clap their hands because God has redeemed Jacob. Job 38:7 recalls that the morning stars sang together when the earth's foundations were laid. The angels of verse 2 appear in Psalm 103:20-21 as those who carry out His word.

The New Testament carries the thought in two directions. Paul writes that the creation is waiting in eager expectation for the revelation of the children of God and will be set free from its bondage to decay, Romans 8:19-21, so the praise of creation is tied to its redemption. And in Colossians 1:16-20 all things in heaven and earth were created through Christ and for Him, and will be reconciled to God through the blood of His cross. In Luke 19:40 Jesus answers those who would silence His disciples with the saying that the stones would cry out, and in Revelation 5:13 every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth, and in the sea joins the song to the Lamb. The horn of verse 14 appears in the song of Zechariah in Luke 1:69.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted to enlarge his hearers' sense of what praise is and who is involved. It is easy to think of praise as a human thing done by people in a building. He wants them to see that the whole universe is saturated with the glory of its Maker and that human worship is the joining of one more voice to a song that is already in progress. The sun that rises on the worshipper's morning, the hail on the roof, and the young cedar on the hill are all in their own way giving God what is due. A person who refuses to praise is the odd one out in a creation that is doing so.

The psalmist also meant to ground the praise in a reason. The summons does not rest on mood. The reason, stated twice, is that God commanded and they were created, and that His name alone is exalted. The things in the list are creatures with a Maker, and they have no standing of their own. The command to praise is therefore a form of truth-telling: to praise the LORD is to say how things are. The sun can be thanked for its warmth, but it is not to be worshipped, and the one who made it deserves the praise.

The ending shows what the hearers are to take home. After the roll call of the cosmos, they are told that the God of everything has raised up strength for 'a people near to Him.' The psalm wants Israel to see itself within this large picture, as the people through whom the Maker is making Himself known, and to sing as those who are close to Him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm is a string of commands, but the commands are of a particular kind. Verses 1 to 4 and 7 to 12 are imperatives addressed to beings that cannot hear in the way people do. No one is expected to preach to the stars. These are poetic commands, a way of saying that the creatures belong to God and that their existence redounds to His glory. The Bible's own idiom backs this reading, since Psalm 19:3 says the heavens have 'no speech or language,' and yet they pour forth knowledge. The commands do not prescribe that believers should address the moon or expect lightning to sing.

The commands to people in verses 11 and 12 are meant at face value. Kings and commoners, young and old, are to praise the LORD, and the verse leaves no one out. That is prescriptive, and it applies to everyone who reads the psalm. It also corrects a narrow idea of who worship is for, since the young men and maidens are as called as the rulers.

The psalm also guards against two misuses. It does not teach that nature is divine, since it addresses nature as a creation under command. It also does not teach that the earth can be used without regard. A creature told to praise its Maker is not mere material to be consumed, and the psalm's regard for the sea creatures, the cedars, and the cattle fits the care for creation that the Bible elsewhere commends, as in Proverbs 12:10.

debates.question: In what sense do sun, moon, stars, and sea creatures 'praise' the LORD?

views.label: A poetic summons: they display His glory and humans give it words
views.case: Psalm 19:1-4 says the heavens declare God's glory without speech, and Romans 1:20 says that creation shows God's power and nature. On this reading the creatures praise simply by being what they are, and the psalm calls on people to put that testimony into words.

views.label: A real response proper to each creature
views.case: Others hold that the Bible speaks of creation responding to God in a way that is more than metaphor, as when the morning stars sing in Job 38:7, the mountains and hills burst into song in Isaiah 55:12, and Jesus says the stones would cry out, Luke 19:40. On this view the praise of creation is a real reply to its Maker that we only partly perceive.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree on the main point. The creatures exist to display the glory of God and are not themselves to be worshipped, and human beings have the unique responsibility to give that glory its voice.

debates.question: What is the horn in verse 14 and who is it?

views.label: God's strengthening of Israel as a people
views.case: In the Old Testament the horn is a symbol of strength and victory, as in Psalm 18:2 and Psalm 75:10. The sentence says that God has raised up a horn for His people, which can mean that He has given them strength and honour, perhaps after a time of weakness.

views.label: A coming king from David's line
views.case: Passages such as 1 Samuel 2:10 and Psalm 132:17 speak of a horn that the LORD will exalt or cause to grow for His anointed. On this reading verse 14 looks toward a Davidic ruler, and Zechariah's song in Luke 1:69 reads it that way, as a horn of salvation raised up in the house of David.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew leaves room for both. Israel's strength and Israel's king are bound together, since the king was the people's representative, and the New Testament sees the fullest answer in the king who is also Israel's salvation.

study.originalLanguages:
The refrain verb is halal, to praise, which gives hallelujah its name. In Psalm 148 it appears in the imperative plural when the psalmist addresses the heavens and the earth, and in a jussive form in verses 5 and 13, 'Let them praise,' in which the command becomes a wish about creation. The same root is used of boasting in the LORD, as in Psalm 34:2, so that to praise Him is to speak of Him with delight.

The word 'hosts' in verse 2 is tsava, from the root of the title 'LORD of Hosts.' It can refer to armies, and it can refer to the heavenly company around the throne, as in 1 Kings 22:19. In Psalm 103:21 it is paired with 'ministers who do His will.' The point is that the angels and the stars are the retinue of the King and not rivals of Him.

Verse 5 says that 'He gave the command and they were created.' The verb for command is tsavah, and the one for created is bara in the passive stem, nivra'u. Bara is the verb of Genesis 1:1, where only God is its subject. The psalmist could have written that the heavens were made, but he chose the verb that the Bible reserves for the work of God alone. The 'decree' of verse 6 is chok, which can mean statute or fixed limit, as in Jeremiah 31:35-36, where the order of sun, moon, and stars is called a fixed statute. The phrase 'will never pass away' uses the verb avar, to cross or pass over, so the decree is a boundary that is not crossed.

In verse 7 the 'great sea creatures' are tanninim, the same word God uses in Genesis 1:21 for the great creatures of the sea. The 'ocean depths' are tehomot, the plural of tehom, the 'deep' of Genesis 1:2. So the primal waters and the monsters in them are the first items on the earthly list. In verse 8 the powerful wind is described as 'fulfilling His word,' with a participle of asah, to do, and the object is 'His word,' davar. The wind does the word as a servant carries out an instruction.

Verse 13 says that 'His name alone is exalted.' The verb is the niphal of sagav, to be set on high, and the phrase 'alone' is levaddo. The same combination appears in Isaiah 2:11 and 2:17, 'the LORD alone will be exalted in that day.' The psalm says that this day has a present reality in praise.

In verse 14 the 'horn' is qeren, an image of strength drawn from the horns of wild oxen, as in Deuteronomy 33:17. The 'saints' are chasidim, from chesed, those who are the objects and the practitioners of covenant loyalty. The clause 'the praise of all His saints' is open to more than one reading: the horn may itself be the praise of the saints, a thing for which they praise Him, or the phrase may stand as a separate statement that the raising of the horn gives all His faithful ones a reason to praise. The people are called 'near to Him,' qerovo, a word from the root of drawing near, as Deuteronomy 4:7 uses of a god near to a nation. The Greek of Luke 1:69 uses keras, the word the Septuagint uses for the horn.

typology.type: The creation summoned to praise, verses 1 to 10
typology.fulfillment: The psalm sets creation's praise on the page before creation's redemption. Paul says that the whole creation was subjected to futility in hope and will be set free from decay into the freedom of the children of God, Romans 8:20-21. The prophets had already pictured the mountains breaking into song when God's people were redeemed, Isaiah 55:12, and Revelation records the song at its fullest, with every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth, and in the sea giving praise to God and to the Lamb, Revelation 5:13. The pattern is thus fulfilled when the Creator becomes the Redeemer of His creation. It falls short in the present, since creation still groans, Romans 8:22, and the full song waits for the age to come.

typology.type: The horn raised up for His people, verse 14
typology.fulfillment: The horn is a standing image of strength and victory that the Old Testament gives to the anointed king, 1 Samuel 2:10 and Psalm 132:17. Zechariah, filled with the Holy Spirit, says that God 'has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David,' Luke 1:69. The correspondence is that the one who gives Israel strength is a person. The escalation is that the horn does not simply defend a nation but brings salvation from sin, Luke 1:77. The type falls short because verse 14 speaks of Israel, whereas Christ's horn reaches the nations, Acts 4:12.

typology.type: The kings and rulers called to praise, verse 11
typology.fulfillment: The psalm calls kings and all peoples to praise. This looks ahead to the day when the nations will come to the light of God's people, Isaiah 60:3, and to the visions of kings of the earth bringing their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24. The call is answered in Christ, to whom every knee is to bow, Philippians 2:10-11, and the first signs of it appear when the Magi from the East come to the child, Matthew 2:11. The type is only partly fulfilled in this age, since many kings still refuse, as Psalm 2:10-12 says, and the final bowing waits for the end.

typology.type: The people near to Him, verse 14
typology.fulfillment: Israel is described as a people near to the LORD, as Deuteronomy 4:7 says that no other nation has a god so near. In Christ the nearness is expanded and made personal. Paul tells Gentiles who were once far away that they have been brought near through the blood of Christ, Ephesians 2:13, and Hebrews says that believers can approach the throne of grace with confidence, Hebrews 4:16. The type is incomplete in the sense that nearness is now by faith and not yet by sight, and the full nearness is the promise that they will see His face, Revelation 22:4.

study.christ:
Psalm 148 leads to Christ first by creation. The psalm's reason for the praise of heaven and earth is that the LORD gave the command and they were created, and the New Testament places the Son in that act. 'In Him all things were created,' says Paul, 'things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities,' Colossians 1:16. The angels, the hosts, the sun, and the sea creatures of the psalm are among these things. Paul also says, 'He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together,' Colossians 1:17, which makes sense of verse 6, where the LORD established them forever by decree. The Gospel of John opens by saying that all things were made through the Word, John 1:3, and Hebrews says that the Son made the universe and upholds all things by His powerful word, Hebrews 1:2-3. When the psalm says, 'He gave the command and they were created,' the apostles hear the voice of the Son.

It leads to Christ by the horn. Zechariah's song, spoken at the birth of John the Baptist and looking beyond him, says that God 'has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David,' Luke 1:69. The Old Testament had attached the horn to David's line in Psalm 132:17, 'There I will make a horn grow for David,' and to the anointed in 1 Samuel 2:10. Psalm 148:14 says that the horn is raised for His people. Luke tells us who the horn is: the child of Mary, a descendant of David, whom the angel said would reign forever, Luke 1:32-33. The strength raised up for Israel is a Saviour.

It leads to Christ by the name that is alone exalted. 'His name alone is exalted,' says the psalm, and Isaiah had said that the LORD alone will be exalted in the day when human pride is brought low, Isaiah 2:11. Paul says that God has exalted Jesus to the highest place and given Him the name above all names, so that every knee should bow 'in heaven and on earth and under the earth,' Philippians 2:9-11. The three realms of the psalm, heaven, earth, and the deep below, are the realms of the bowing knees. Paul applies to Christ the language that the Old Testament reserved for the LORD, and the psalm's exclusive praise is therefore not diluted but fulfilled.

It leads to Christ by the people near to Him. The 'people near to Him' in verse 14 are Israel, and Paul says that Gentiles who were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ, Ephesians 2:13. The nearness that was a privilege of one nation becomes a gift for all who are in the Son.

A caution is needed. Psalm 148 does not name the Messiah and has no hidden coded details, and creation's praise is not a prediction. The apostolic reading is that the one by whom and for whom the creation was made is the Son, and the horn raised up is the Son. The texts that carry the link are Colossians 1, Luke 1, and Philippians 2, so the reading rests on what the New Testament says and not on a guess.
study.god:
The first thing the psalm teaches about God is that He is Creator by word. 'He gave the command and they were created,' verse 5. The sentence has an astonishing ease about it. The sun, the stars, and the ocean depths did not come about by struggle or by accident but by an order given. This is the God of Genesis 1 and the God of Psalm 33:9, 'He spoke, and it came to be.' It means that no creature is a rival to Him, and nothing in the universe is an independent power.

He is also the one who sustains. The decree of verse 6 means that the order of the heavens is not left to run on its own. 'He established them forever and ever.' The regularity of the sun and the seasons is a faithfulness that flows from His commitment, and Jeremiah 33:25 treats it as the pledge of a covenant. The same God who gave the order keeps it, and the psalm presents that dependability as a reason to praise.

He is the God above all other claims. 'His name alone is exalted; His splendor is above the earth and the heavens,' verse 13. The word 'alone' guards the psalm from any suggestion that a creature, however grand, shares His glory. This is the most basic kind of monotheism, that He is the one to whom all praise ultimately goes. His splendor is not located in a place, since it is above the heavens as well as above the earth, which means that He is not contained by the universe He made.

He is God of the particular. After the grand sweep of the psalm, verse 14 mentions a people near to Him and a horn raised for them. The God who commands angels and stars has also chosen to be near to a people and to strengthen them. The psalm's greatest point is that vastness and nearness belong together.

He is the God who is pleased to be praised, and not out of need. Acts 17:25 says that He is not served by human hands as if He needed anything, because He gives everyone life and breath. The praise of the psalm is not feeding Him, and it is a fitting answer to what He has done. That is also why it can be asked of everything He made, since the praise does not add to Him and is the natural fullness of a creation that knows its Maker.

He is a God who rules the powerful. The kings and princes of verse 11 stand alongside the young men and maidens. His kingship is above every human throne, and the rulers of the earth are summoned like everyone else.

For worship, the psalm teaches that praise is a corporate and cosmic activity in which each person has a place. It trains the worshipper to see lightning, hail, cedars, and sparrows as fellow worshippers and not as raw material. It also gives a reason for praise that can survive hard seasons, because the grounds of the praise are the command that made the world and the decree that holds it, and neither depends on how the singer feels.

crossReferences.note: God creates the great sea creatures and every living thing that moves in the water. Psalm 148:7 names these same creatures first in its earthly list, so the monsters of the deep appear as creatures that praise and not as rivals of God.

The heavens were made by the word of the LORD and the stars by the breath of His mouth, and 'He spoke, and it came to be.' It is the clearest parallel to verse 5, and it explains why the psalm can summon creation, since what was made by a command can be commanded.

The heavens declare the glory of God, without speech or language, yet their voice goes out to all the earth. It shows how silent creation can be said to praise, which clarifies the way Psalm 148 calls on beings that do not speak.

When the foundations of the earth were laid, the morning stars sang together and the sons of God shouted for joy. It gives a picture of the creation's first praise, so that Psalm 148's chorus is a renewal of a song that began on the day the world was made.

The angels, who carry out His word, the hosts, who do His will, and all His works are called to bless the LORD. It is the nearest parallel to the heavenly list of verses 1 and 2, and it shows what the angels are for: they serve the word and join the praise.

The mountains and hills burst into song and the trees clap their hands when God's people go out with joy. The prophet links the praise of creation to the redemption of God's people, a link that Psalm 148 makes by closing with the horn raised up for Israel.

The covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth is the guarantee that God will not reject the descendants of Jacob and David. It explains how the decree of verse 6 that will never pass away supports the promise to Israel in verse 14.

The creation waits in eager expectation to be set free from its bondage to decay. Paul gives a reason why creation's praise is not yet perfect, and shows that its freedom is bound up with the revelation of God's children, which is the hope inside the psalm.

All things in heaven and on earth were created in Christ and through Him and for Him, and in Him they hold together. It gives the apostolic reading of verses 5 and 6, so that the command that made the angels, stars, and sea creatures is the Son's.

Zechariah, filled with the Spirit, says that God has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David, as He spoke through the holy prophets. It picks up the horn of verse 14 and names its house, joining the psalm to the expected Davidic king.

God gives Jesus the name above all names, so that every knee should bow in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. It echoes the psalm's claim that the LORD's name alone is exalted, and places Jesus inside that exaltation.

Every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth, and in the sea sings praise to the One on the throne and to the Lamb. The scope of the praise matches the scope of Psalm 148, and the Lamb now stands beside the One who is praised.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 148 sits on the first page of the story, where God speaks and the heavens and earth appear, Genesis 1, and it reads that page as a call to worship. The psalm borrows the vocabulary of the days, the heavens and their lights, the waters and their creatures, the land and its plants, the animals, and finally humanity. The psalm takes the creation account and shows its purpose. The world was made to be full of praise, and humanity was made to be the voice of that praise.

The story that follows is the story of how that purpose was broken. In Genesis 3 the human voice turned away, and the creation was caught up in the consequences, subjected to futility and bondage to decay, Romans 8:20-21. Psalm 148 is a reminder of the original order, and it holds the hope of restoration. The song of the psalm is not the song of a perfect world but a summons from within a world that still groans, which is why it reaches toward a day when the praise will be complete.

It also sets Israel in the middle of the story. The closing verse speaks of a people near to Him, and the horn raised for them is a promise of strength. Israel is the people through whom the Creator works to restore the creation. The promise to Abraham, that all families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3, is the means by which the nations who are summoned in verse 11 come to praise. The horn from David's line, anticipated in 1 Samuel 2:10 and Psalm 132:17, is the one through whom the restoration comes.

The story reaches its turn in Christ. The Son through whom all things were made, Colossians 1:16, entered His own creation, Zechariah's horn of salvation was raised up in the house of David, Luke 1:69, and the one who made the stars and the sea was found in a boat commanding the wind to be still, Mark 4:39. His death, Paul says, reconciles to God all things, whether on earth or in heaven, Colossians 1:20, so that the redemption is not only of people but of the creation that had been caught up in their fall.

The story ends with the psalm fulfilled. In Revelation 5:13 every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth, and in the sea sings to the One on the throne and to the Lamb, and in Revelation 7:9-12 a multitude from every nation joins the angels in praise. The kings of the earth bring their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24, the curse is gone, Revelation 22:3, and the creation that was made to praise does so without a discordant voice. The summons that opened with 'Hallelujah' is answered by everything that has breath, as Psalm 150:6 says.

sermon.title: He Commanded and They Were Created
sermon.why: Piper opens a series on redemptive history with Psalm 148:5, He commanded and they were created, unpacking the doctrine of creation and its implications, that God owns, purposes, and sustains all He has made, the very truth this psalm summons all creation to praise Him for.

quiz.q: Who is summoned to praise in verses 1-4?

options.text: The heavens, the highest places, all His angels and heavenly hosts, sun, moon, and shining stars.
options.note: These verses summon the whole heavenly realm to praise before the psalm turns to earth.

options.text: Only the priests serving in the temple.
options.note: The summons here is cosmic, angels and heavenly bodies, not limited to the priesthood.

options.text: Only the kings and rulers of the earth.
options.note: Kings and rulers appear later, in verse 11, not in this opening summons from the heavens.

options.text: The heavens in general terms, without any specific beings named.
options.note: The psalm is quite specific, naming angels, hosts, sun, moon, and stars by name.

quiz.q: Why must creation praise the LORD, according to verses 5-6?

options.text: Because He commanded and they were created, and He established them by a decree that will never pass away.
options.note: Creation's existence and stability are grounded entirely in God's command and decree.

options.text: Because creation evolved into its present form by chance.
options.note: The text explicitly attributes creation to God's command, not chance.

options.text: Because creation praises itself, apart from any Creator.
options.note: The praise is directed to the LORD as the one who commanded creation into being.

options.text: Because creation was made long ago but is no longer sustained by God.
options.note: Verse 6 stresses that God established creation forever and ever, ongoing sustaining, not a one-time act now abandoned.

quiz.q: What does verse 14 say the LORD has done for His people?

options.text: He has raised up a horn for them, the praise of all His saints, of Israel, a people near to Him.
options.note: This closing verse names Israel's special nearness to God and the strength, or rescuer, He has raised up for them.

options.text: He has abandoned them to their enemies.
options.note: The verse describes the opposite, God raising up strength and drawing His people near.

options.text: He has raised up a horn for every nation equally, without distinction.
options.note: The verse specifically names Israel as the people near to Him, not every nation without distinction.

options.text: He has given them wealth but withheld His presence.
options.note: The verse specifically emphasizes nearness to God, not merely material blessing.

quiz.q: How does Luke 1:69 connect to this psalm's image of a horn?

options.text: Zechariah's song applies the same image directly to Jesus, God has raised up a horn of salvation for us.
options.note: Luke 1:69 draws directly on this Old Testament image of a horn as a rescuer king.

options.text: Luke 1:69 rejects the image of a horn entirely.
options.note: Luke 1:69 embraces and fulfills the image rather than rejecting it.

options.text: The horn in Luke 1:69 refers only to a literal musical instrument.
options.note: Both texts use horn as a symbol of strength and rescue, not a literal musical instrument.

options.text: The connection is possible but widely disputed among scholars.
options.note: The verbal and thematic parallel is a well recognized, direct scriptural echo.

quiz.q: What is the range of humanity summoned to praise in verses 11-12?

options.text: Kings and all peoples, princes and rulers, young men and maidens, old and young together.
options.note: The summons spans every social rank and every age, leaving no one excluded.

options.text: Only the wealthy and powerful.
options.note: The text specifically includes young and old, common people alongside rulers.

options.text: Only the priests and Levites.
options.note: The summons is to all humanity, not a specific religious class.

options.text: Kings and rulers only, with the common people left out.
options.note: The text explicitly adds all peoples, young men, maidens, old and young, not rulers alone.

questions: This psalm summons the whole created order, angels, stars, weather, animals, and every kind of person, to praise God. What part of creation, or your own life, tends to go silent instead of praising Him?
Verse 14 says God has raised up a horn, a rescuer, for His people. Where do you need to remember that God has already secured your rescue in Christ?
Kings, rulers, young and old alike are called to praise, verses 11-12. Is there a category of person you unconsciously exclude from worship or from the gospel's reach?
If all creation, seen and unseen, exists to display God's glory, how does that reshape the way you see an ordinary part of your day, weather, work, or a walk outside?
This psalm's praise anticipates Revelation 5:13's vision of every creature praising God and the Lamb. How does that future hope change how you worship today?

translationNotes.note: The highest places, or the heights, renders a Hebrew phrase for the upper heavens, associated with God's own presence and the angels.
Waters above the skies reflects the ancient Hebrew picture of the created order in Genesis 1:6-8, waters separated by an expanse, here summoned along with everything else to praise their Maker.
Horn renders qeren, an image of strength drawn from an animal's horn; it becomes a title for the promised rescuer king, as in Luke 1:69.
